title: Snowflake SQL Best Practices for Petabyte-Scale Queries
description: Critical optimization rules for generating efficient SQL on Snowflake's micro-partition architecture

rules: Snowflake stores data in compressed, columnar, immutable micro-partitions (~16MB each)
Every query tries to SKIP unnecessary partitions using metadata (min/max values per partition)
Your #1 goal: maximize partition pruning = minimize scanned data = minimize cost
NEVER apply functions to filter columns (e.g., YEAR(sale_date) = 2026) — this prevents pruning
USE range predicates instead: sale_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
Pre-filter dimension tables in CTEs, then join the small result to fact tables — this enables the optimizer to prune fact-table partitions via join keys
Snowflake is columnar — only queried columns are decompressed and scanned
NEVER use SELECT * — each extra column increases bytes scanned and cost
Only select columns you actually need for the answer
At PB scale, an unnecessary column can add terabytes of scanning
AGGREGATE fact tables by surrogate keys FIRST, THEN join to dimensions for labels
Filter BEFORE joining — reduce row counts in CTEs before any JOIN
Bad: SELECT dim.name, SUM(fact.amount) FROM fact JOIN dim GROUP BY dim.name
Good: WITH agg AS (SELECT fk, SUM(amount) FROM fact GROUP BY fk) SELECT dim.name, agg.total FROM agg JOIN dim ON ...
This pattern reduces shuffle, prevents spilling, and enables better parallelism
When query memory exceeds warehouse memory, Snowflake spills to local disk then remote storage
Spilling DESTROYS performance — queries can be 10-100x slower
Solutions: pre-aggregate in CTEs, filter early, reduce join cardinality
Check Query Profile for 'Bytes Spilled to Local/Remote Storage'
Large JOINs on unfiltered fact tables are the #1 cause of spilling
Use QUALIFY instead of nested subqueries for window-function filters: SELECT ... QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 10
Use NULLIF() to prevent division-by-zero in rate calculations
Use IFF() or CASE for conditional aggregation instead of multiple scans
Use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT() when exact distinct counts are not required — much faster at scale
Use :: for casting (e.g., column::DATE) which is cleaner and idiomatic Snowflake
NEVER use correlated subqueries against fact tables — resolve values in a CTE first
AVOID COUNT(DISTINCT surrogate_key) on billions of rows — use COUNT(*) after GROUP BY
NEVER query a fact table without a date filter — it will scan ALL partitions
AVOID repeated CTE references that cause recomputation — split into sequential CTEs
AVOID UNION when UNION ALL suffices — UNION forces a sort/distinct operation
AVOID ORDER BY on large intermediate results — only ORDER on final output
Snowflake distributes data across nodes — large joins trigger repartitioning and network transfer
Always filter BOTH sides of a join as much as possible before the join
Put the smaller table/CTE as the build side (Snowflake usually auto-detects this)
For SCD Type 2 dimensions, always filter REC_END_DATE IS NULL to get current version only
Check for NULL foreign keys before joining (e.g., SS_CUSTOMER_SK IS NOT NULL)
Snowflake caches results — identical queries return instantly if data hasn't changed
Cache invalidates if: underlying data changes, query text changes, or 24 hours pass
Deterministic queries on stable tables benefit most from caching
Do not add unnecessary randomness (e.g., CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) if not needed
